title: In re Stavros Anthony, Case No. 25-024C (Lieutenant Governor)
text:
STATE OF NEVADA
BEFORE THE NEVADA COMMISSION ON ETHICS
In re Stavros Anthony, Ethics Complaint
Lieutenant Governor, Case No. 25-024C
State of Nevada,
Subject. /
OPINION
I. INTRODUCTION AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Pursuant to NRS 291A.710(1)(b), an Ethics Complaint was filed with the Nevada
Commission on Ethics (“Commission”) on February 27, 2025 by a member of the public
alleging that Stavros Anthony (Anthony”) violated various provisions of the Ethics in
Government Law set forth in NRS Chapter 281A (“Ethics Law”)
The Commission issued its Order on Jurisdiction and Investigation and Notice of
Additional Issues and Facts on April 14, 2025, accepting jurisdiction and directing the
Executive Director to investigate Anthony’s alleged violations of NRS 281A.400(7). The
Commission also found sufficient evidence to accept jurisdiction and investigate
additional issues and facts pursuant to NAC 281A.415 for violations of NRS 281.400(2)
and (9).
On April 15, 2025, the Commission served Anthony via certified mail with a Notice
of Complaint and Investigation, providing him with its Order on Jurisdiction and
Investigation and Notice of Additional Issues and Facts (“Order and Notice”). The Order
and Notice provided Anthony with notice of his alleged violations of NRS 281A.400(2), (7)
and (9) on the following basis:
Specifically, the additional issues and facts discovered during the
jurisdictional review process include use of government social media
accounts belonging to the Office of the Lt. Governor, the Office of Small
Business Advocacy, and the Nevada Division of Tourism to amplify and
promote private non-governmental political and personal accounts of
Stavros Anthony, Sarah Johnson, and others. The primary focus of the
Complaint allegations related to the Task Force is the determination about
whether the Task Force is a personal interest or an interest of the Office of
the Lieutenant Governor. See In re Hammargren, Comm’n Op. No. 95-35
(1996), In re Augustine, Comm’n Op. No. 04-47 (2004), and In re Matson,
Comm’n Op. No 11-67C (2014).
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 1 of 20

The Commission served Anthony with a Second Notice of Additional Issues and
Facts on June 25, 2025, providing additional information regarding Anthony’s alleged
violations of NRS 281A.400(2) and (7).
On August 20, 2025, the Commission’s Review Panel (“Panel”)1 issued a Review
Panel Determination, unanimously finding that the facts in this matter established credible
evidence to support a determination that just and sufficient cause existed for the
Commission to render an opinion regarding Anthony’s alleged violations of NRS
281A.400(2), (7) and (9).
The Panel further determined pursuant to NRS 281A.730(5) that Anthony’s
conduct could be appropriately addressed through corrective action under a deferral
agreement in which Anthony would have been required to agree to the following terms:
1) Comply with the Ethics Law from the date of the Review Panel’s approval of
the deferral agreement for a period to conclude the day after the November
2026 election or one year from the approval date of the agreement, whichever
is later (“Deferral Term”), without being the subject of another complaint arising
from an alleged violation of the Ethics Law and for which a review panel
determines there is just and sufficient cause for the Commission to render an
opinion in the matter;
2) Schedule and attend training as approved by the Executive Director for
Subject’s entire office staff within 60 days of the approval date of the
agreement. Subject will also ensure any new staff hired during the Deferral
Term and any campaign staff receive Ethics Law training within 30 days of their
start date;
3) Ensure that no official agency social media accounts or other communication
platforms (website, newsletters, etc.) are used to amplify or promote Subject’s
private or campaign accounts or the campaign accounts of any other
individuals;
4) Communicate to state and local agencies that Subject frequently works with
that they must tag Subject’s official social media accounts and not his private
personal accounts in any postings and communications;
5) Draft and adopt a social media policy for the Office of the Lieutenant Governor
that expressly prohibits use of government accounts to promote political
campaigns; and
6) Certify in writing that Subject has read and understands the Improper Benefits
chapter of the Ethics Manual within 30 days of approval of this agreement.
Anthony declined to enter into the deferral agreement on the terms set forth by the
Panel. The Commission issued a Referral Order on September 10, 2025, referring this
matter to the full Commission for an adjudicatory hearing pursuant to NRS 281A.750(6)
regarding Anthony’s alleged violations of NRS 281A.400(2), (7) and (9).
1 Chair Scott Scherer and Commissioners Teresa Lowry and John Miller served on the Review Panel and
are precluded by NRS 281A.220(4) from participation in further matters after issuance of the Panel
Determination.
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 2 of 20

On November 13, 2025, the Commission issued its Discovery and Scheduling
Order (“DSO”), setting a hearing on dispositive motions for March 18, 2026 and an
adjudicatory hearing for May 20, 2026.
Each Party filed a motion for summary judgment on February 11, 2026, oppositions
to the motions on March 2, 2026, and replies in support of the motions on March 4, 2026.
The briefing on summary judgment from both parties contained various exhibits and
documents in support of the respective motions.
On March 18, 2026, the Commission heard oral argument on the Parties’ motions
for summary judgment. At the conclusion of the oral argument and after fully considering
the record, testimony, evidence and arguments of the parties, in accordance with the
requirements of the law including, without limitation, the mitigating factors set forth in NRS
281A.775, the Commission deliberated and granted in part both parties’ motions for
summary judgment, approving on the record the finding of one non-willful violation of NRS
281A.400(2) and one willful and one non-willful violation of NRS 281A.400(7). The
Commission found no violation of NRS 281A.400(9).
The Commission imposed on Anthony a civil penalty in the amount of $3,000 for
his willful violation of NRS 281A.400(7). The Commission also admonished Anthony,
required him to complete ethics training selected by the Executive Director within 60 days
of the written decision being issued and required him to develop social media policies for
the Lieutenant Governor’s Office and the Office of Small Business Administration.
The Commission now renders this written opinion setting forth its formal findings
of fact and conclusions of law in compliance with NRS 233B.125 and NAC 281A.473.
II. FINDINGS OF FACT
The Commission granted summary judgment in favor of the Executive Director as
to NRS 281A.400(2) and (7) and in favor of Anthony as to NRS 281A.400(9) because
there are no material issues of fact remaining in dispute and summary judgment was
warranted as a matter of law. Anthony’s conduct is deemed to constitute one non-willful
violation of NRS 281A.400(2) and one non-willful violation of NRS 281A.400(7). Anthony’s
conduct is further deemed to constitute one willful violation of NRS 281A.400(7), as more
particularly set forth in this opinion, which determination of willfulness considered the
mitigating factors set forth in NRS 281A.475, and resulted in a fine imposed in the amount
of $3,000. In rendering this opinion, the Commission determines the following facts to be
established under the preponderance of evidence standard set forth in NRS 281A.790(9),
NRS 281A.765, and NRS 233B.125:
1. Anthony currently serves as the elected Lieutenant Governor of Nevada.
He has held this position since assuming office on January 2, 2023.
2. Anthony earns a salary in connection with his position as the Lieutenant
Governor.
3. Anthony is currently running for reelection.
4. The Lieutenant Governor is a public officer as defined in NRS 281A.160.
5. The Lieutenant Governor serves in various statutory capacities, including:
Opinion

Page 3 of 20

a. President of the Nevada Senate (Nev. Const. art. V, § 17);
b. Chair of the Nevada Commission on Tourism (NRS 231.8121);
c. Chair of the Advisory Board on Outdoor Recreation (NRS
407A.575);
d. Member of the Board of Transportation (NRS 408.106);
e. Member of the Board of Economic Development (NRS 231.033);
f. Member of the Executive Branch Audit Committee (NRS
353A.038); and
g. Trustee on the Nevada Employee Savings Trust Board (NRS
353D.200).
6. As Lieutenant Governor, Anthony oversees the Office of the Lieutenant
Governor (“LG Office”) along with the Office of Small Business Advocacy
(“OSBA”).
7. As Lt. Governor, Anthony sits on various boards and commissions including
the State Board of Transportation, the State Board of Economic
Development, the Advisory Board on Outdoor Recreation and the Nevada
Commission on Tourism.
8. Rudy Pamintuan (“Pamintuan”), Sarah Johnson (“Johnson”) and Garret
Tamagni (“Tamagni”) were at all material times public employees and
subordinates of Anthony, working either in the LG Office or the OSBA.
9. Anthony received proper notice of his alleged violations of NRS
281A.400(2), (7) and (9) in the Commission’s April 15, 2025 Notice and
Order.
Social Media
10. The LG Office maintains a government X (formerly Twitter) social media
account: @NevadaLtGov. The description for this account states, “Official
account for Nevada's Office of the Lieutenant Governor” and links to the
official state government page for the LG Office.
11. The OSBA maintains a government X social media account: @osbanv. This
account and links to the official state government page for the OSBA.
12. The @NevadaLtGov and @osbanv government X accounts are both official
government resources.
13. The OSBA was funded from a specific federal grant related to recovery from
the COVID-19 pandemic.
14. Neither the LG Office nor the OSBA have a policy permitting use of
government social media accounts for amplification of private personal
accounts.
15. Anthony maintains a personal X social media account: @StavrosAnthony.
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 4 of 20

16. The @StavrosAnthony account is used to promote Anthony’s personal
political interests, including his reelection campaign for Lieutenant
Governor.
17. LG Office staff, specifically Tamagni, developed content that was posted to
the @StavrosAnthony personal social media account while being paid to
work for the LG Office. Specifically, Tamagni used LG Office work hours to
create social media posts that were posted to the @StavrosAnthony
account on the following dates:
a. October 10, 2024;
b. October 24, 2024;
c. April 4, 2025;
d. May 1, 2025; and
e. May 12, 2025.
18. The @osbanv and @NevadaLtGov official social media accounts both
reposted X posts originally posted to the @StavrosAnthony personal social
media account, including posts in support of Anthony’s reelection
campaign, amplifying those posts to the viewers of the LG Office and OSBA
official government account pages.
Task Force
19. In late 2024, Anthony directed his LG Office and OSBA staff to establish a
Task Force for the Protection of Women’s Sports (“Task Force”).
20. The Task Force is its own entity and not a function of the LG Office or OSBA.
Neither Anthony nor the staff of the LG Office or the OSBA considered the
Task Force to be a part of or a function of either office.
21. Johnson used OSBA staff time and email systems to set-up and coordinate
the efforts of the Task Force.
22. LG Office and OSBA staff created talking points, press releases, and other
materials in support of the Task Force, including “some phone calls, 3 or 4
flyers, limited emails, and some social media”.
23. The @osbanv and @NevadaLtGov accounts posted and reposted X posts
related to the Task Force, promoting it via their government X feeds. This
included reposting X posts regarding the Task Force from Anthony’s
personal @StavrosAnthony account.
24. Anthony never requested specific state funding for the activities of the Task
Force.
25. Anthony never sought statutory changes to establish the Task Force.
26. Anthony never presented the work of the Task Force to any of the boards
or commissions he sits on as Lieutenant Governor.
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 5 of 20

27. The boards and commissions on which Anthony sits as Lieutenant
Governor do not work on or are related to children’s or women’s sports.
28. Anthony has not proposed or sponsored any legislation regarding the issues
addressed by the Task Force, and the work of the Task Force was primarily
limited to lobbying the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association for rule
changes.
29. Anthony testified before the Joint Meeting of the Senate Committee on
Finance and Assembly Committee on Ways and Means on February 5,
2025, stating "I decided I was very passionate about protecting female
athletes. I wanted to support the University of Nevada, Reno (UNR)
volleyball team who came out very courageously on their stand. That is why
I created this task force."
III. RELEVANT STATUTES
A. NRS 281A.020(1) – Duty to Avoid Conflicts:
1. It is hereby declared to be the public policy of this State that:
(a) A public office is a public trust and shall be held for the sole benefit
of the people.
(b) A public officer or employee must commit himself or herself to avoid
conflicts between the private interests of the public officer or employee and
those of the general public whom the public officer or employee serves.
B. NRS 281A.400(2) – Use of Government Position to Secure or Grant
“Unwarranted” Privileges, Preferences, or Advantages:
A public officer or employee shall not use the public officer’s or employee’s
position in government to secure or grant unwarranted privileges, preferences,
exemptions or advantages for the public officer or employee, any business
entity in which the public officer or employee has a significant pecuniary interest
or any person to whom the public officer or employee has a commitment in a
private capacity. As used in this subsection, “unwarranted” means without
justification or adequate reason.
C. NRS 281A.400(7) – Improper use of Government Resources and Property:
Except for State Legislators who are subject to the restrictions set forth in
subsection 8, a public officer or employee shall not use governmental time,
property, equipment or other facility to benefit a significant personal or
pecuniary interest of the public officer or employee or any person to whom the
public officer or employee has a commitment in a private capacity. This
subsection does not prohibit:
(a) A limited use of governmental property, equipment or other facility for
personal purposes if:
(1) The public officer or employee who is responsible for and has
authority to authorize the use of such property, equipment or other facility
has established a policy allowing the use or the use is necessary as a result
of emergency circumstances;
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 6 of 20

(2) The use does not interfere with the performance of the public
officer’s or employee’s public duties;
(3) The cost or value related to the use is nominal; and
(4) The use does not create the appearance of impropriety;
(b) The use of mailing lists, computer data or other information lawfully
obtained from a governmental agency which is available to members of the
general public for nongovernmental purposes; or
(c) The use of telephones or other means of communication if there is not
a special charge for that use.
→If a governmental agency incurs a cost as a result of a use that is authorized
pursuant to this subsection or would ordinarily charge a member of the general
public for the use, the public officer or employee shall promptly reimburse the
cost or pay the charge to the governmental agency.
D. NRS 281A.400(9) – Use of Government Position to Attempt to Benefit
Personal or Pecuniary Interests Through Influence of a Subordinate:
A public officer or employee shall not attempt to benefit a significant personal
or pecuniary interest of the public officer or employee or any person to whom
the public officer or employee has a commitment in a private capacity through
the influence of a subordinate.
E. NRS 281A.775 – Standards for Determining Willful Violation:
1. The Commission, in determining whether a violation of this chapter is a
willful violation and, if so, the penalty to be imposed on a public officer or
employee or former public officer or employee pursuant to NRS 281A.785 or
281A.790, or the review panel, in determining whether to approve a deferral
agreement regarding an alleged violation, shall consider, without limitation:
(a) The seriousness of the violation or alleged violation, including, without
limitation, the nature, circumstances, extent and gravity of the violation or
alleged violation;
(b) The number and history of previous warnings, letters of caution or
instruction, deferral agreements or violations or alleged violations of the
provisions of this chapter relating to the public officer or employee;
(c) The cost to conduct the investigation and any meetings, hearings or
other proceedings relating to the violation or alleged violation;
(d) Any mitigating factors, including, without limitation, any self-reporting,
prompt correction of the violation or alleged violation, any attempts to rectify
the violation or alleged violation before any ethics complaint is filed and any
cooperation by the public officer or employee in resolving the ethics complaint;
(e) Any restitution or reimbursement paid to parties affected by the
violation or alleged violation;
(f) The extent of any financial gain resulting from the violation or alleged
violation; and
(g) Any other matter justice may require.
2. The factors set forth in this section are not exclusive or exhaustive, and the
Commission or the review panel, as appropriate, may consider other factors in
the disposition of the matter if they bear a reasonable relationship to the
determination of the severity of the violation or alleged violation.
3. In applying the factors set forth in this section, the Commission or the
review panel, as appropriate, shall treat comparable situations in a comparable
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 7 of 20

manner and shall ensure that the disposition of the matter bears a reasonable
relationship to the severity of the violation or alleged violation.
F. Definitions Applicable to Willfulness Determination:
NRS 281A.105 “Intentionally” defined. “Intentionally” means voluntarily or
deliberately, rather than accidentally or inadvertently. The term does not
require proof of bad faith, ill will, evil intent, or malice.
NRS 281A.115 “Knowingly” defined. “Knowingly imports a knowledge that
the facts exist which constitute the act or omission, and does not require
knowledge of the prohibition against the act or omission. Knowledge of any
particular fact may be inferred from the knowledge of such other facts as should
put an ordinarily prudent person upon inquiry.
NRS 281A.170 “Willful violation” defined. “Willful violation” means a
violation where the public officer or employee:
Acted intentionally or knowingly; or
Was in a situation where this chapter imposed a duty to act and the public
officer or employee intentionally and knowingly failed to act in the manner
required by this chapter,  unless the Commission determines, after applying
the factors set forth in NRS 281A.775, that the public officer’s or employee’s
act or failure to act has not resulted in a sanctionable violation of this chapter.
G. NRS 281A.785 – Remedies for Violations of Ethics Law:
1. Except as otherwise provided in this section, in proceedings concerning an
ethics complaint, the Commission, based on a finding that a violation of this
chapter has been proven, or the review panel, as part of the terms and
conditions of a deferral agreement, may, in addition to any other penalty
provided by law and in accordance with the provisions of NRS 281A.775:
***
(b) Publicly admonish, reprimand or censure the public officer or
employee.
***
2. In carrying out the provisions of subsection 1, the Commission, based on
a finding that a violation of this chapter has been proven, or the review panel,
as part of the terms and conditions of a deferral agreement, may publicly:
(a) Admonish a public officer or employee if it is determined
that the public officer or employee has violated any provision of this
chapter, but the violation is not willful, or if such an admonishment is
imposed as part of the terms and conditions of a deferral agreement. An
admonishment is a written expression of disapproval of the conduct of the
public officer or employee.
(b) Reprimand a public officer or employee if it is determined
that the public officer or employee has willfully violated any provision of
this chapter, but there is no evidence that the willful violation involved bad
faith, malicious intent or knowing or reckless disregard of the law, or if
such a reprimand is imposed as part of the terms and conditions of a
deferral agreement. A reprimand is a severe written reproof for the
conduct of the public officer or employee.
(c) Censure a public officer or employee if it is determined that
the public officer or employee has willfully violated any provision of this
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 8 of 20

chapter and there is evidence that the willful violation involved bad faith,
malicious intent or knowing or reckless disregard of the law or there are
no substantial mitigating factors pursuant to NRS 281A.775 for the willful
violation, or if such a censure is imposed as part of the terms and
conditions of a deferral agreement. A censure is a formal written
condemnation of the conduct of the public officer or employee.
H. NRS 281A.790 – Civil Penalties for Willful Violations:
1. In addition to any other penalties provided by law and in accordance with
the provisions of NRS 281A.775, the Commission may impose on a public
officer or employee or former public officer or employee civil penalties:
(a) Not to exceed $5,000 for a first willful violation of this chapter;
(b) Not to exceed $10,000 for a separate act or event that
constitutes a second willful violation of this chapter; and
(c) Not to exceed $25,000 for a separate act or event that constitutes
a third willful violation of this chapter.
***
9. A finding by the Commission that a public officer or employee has violated
any provision of this chapter must be supported by a preponderance of the
evidence unless a greater burden is otherwise prescribed by law.
IV. DECISION
The Ethics Law is designed to preserve the public trust and ensure that public
officers and employees maintain proper separation between their public duties and
private interests. See NRS 281A.020. In furtherance of State policy to protect the public
trust, the Code of Ethical Standards was enacted to require proper separation of private
interests and commitments from public duties. See NRS 281A.400.
Pursuant to NRS 281A.280, the Commission has jurisdiction over public officers,
as that term is defined in NRS 281A.160, if their conduct implicates a violation of Nevada’s
Ethics in Government Law, set forth in NRS Chapter 281A (“Ethics Law”). Anthony does
not contest jurisdiction in these proceedings, or the fact that he was a public officer under
NRS 281A.160, at all relevant times and the Commission has found that Nevada’s
Lieutenant Governor is a public officer to purposes of the Ethics Law. See In re
Hammargren, Comm’n Op. No. 95-35 (1996).
Once a complaint is referred to the Commission for proceedings, the Commission
may rule on a dispositive motion. See NAC 281A.442. Accordingly, the Commission has
jurisdiction over Anthony and is provided authority to consider the motions and issue this
order. In considering whether there is a violation of the Ethics Law, NRS 281A.480(9)
establishes the burden of proof to be a “preponderance of the evidence,” which means
that the evidence is sufficient for the Commission to determine that the existence of the
contested fact is more probable than the nonexistence of the contested fact. See NRS
233B.0375.
In considering the parties’ motions for summary judgment, the Commission
considered the record before it, including without limitation, the Complaint, Anthony’s
Responses to the Complaint, filed pleadings and supportive evidence in the form of public
records, depositions, discovery requests and responses. Further, each party presented
oral arguments to the Commission during the public meeting in support of their respective
motion.
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 9 of 20

As discussed below, the Commission concludes that Anthony committed one non-
willful violation of NRS 281A.400(2) and one willful violation of NRS 281A.400(7) based
on his use of state staff, time and resources to create and amplify his personal campaign
social media posts and one non-willful violation of NRS 281A.400(7) related to his use of
state email systems, government social media accounts, letterhead, and seal in support
of the Task Force. The Commission further finds that Anthony did not violate NRS
281A.400(9).
A. VIOLATION OF NRS 281A.400(2) – USE OF GOVERNMENT POSITION
TO SECURE OR GRANT “UNWARRANTED” PRIVILEGES,
PREFERENCES, OR ADVANTAGES
As relevant here, a violation of NRS 281A.400(2) occurs when a public officer uses
his position in government to secure or grant himself an unwarranted privilege or
advantage.2 At issue in this matter is whether Anthony’s use of LT Office and OSBA staff,
time and resources to create personal social media posts and repost and amplify his
personal campaign social media posts from @StavrosAnthony on the LG Office and
OSBA government accounts conferred an unwarranted privilege or advantage on
Anthony in violation NRS 281A.400(2).
The Executive Director argued that Anthony granted himself the unwarranted
privilege or advantage of (1) using official government social media accounts, and the
appearance of official sanction and constituent reach that those accounts bring with them,
to benefit his personal interests; and (2) using state employees to create social media
content for his personal, campaign social media accounts. Anthony contends that he did
not violate NRS 281A.400(2) because his use of government staff, time and resources to
create and repost his personal of social media posts to government accounts in support
of his campaign was not an unwarranted benefit.
The Commission has repeatedly held that “public officers and employees are not
entitled to take advantage of public resources to support their own campaign or other
political interests” and cautioned against any attempt, even an incidental one, to bolster
a political endorsement or campaign by the use of a public office and associated
accouterments or any governmental property, equipment or resources.3 In re Public
Officer, Comm’n Op. No. 19-124A (2020) (“19-124A”). “Such uses provide the impression
that the public officer is acting in an official capacity implicating NRS 281A.400(2).” Id.
Although the Commission has determined that an elected public officer’s use of
only their name and title to promote a campaign is not precluded by the Ethics Law, any
use of an official position, including any accouterments of public office, to bolster the
political endorsement is inappropriate because it creates the impression of government
sanction and therefore creates an unwarranted benefit to the public officer. See In re
Public Officer, Comm’n Op. No. 25-206A (2025); In re Seaman, Comm’n Op. No. 23-143
(2024) (“Seaman”); In re Kirkland, Comm’n Op. No. 98-041 (1999). “The power and
prestige of the [public] office” may not be used to bolster private political endorsements.”
In re Antinoro, Comm’n Op. Nos. 18-031C/18-052C (2019) (“Antinoro”), at p. 6, citing In
re Kuzanek, Comm’n Op. No. 14-61C (2014).
2 NRS 281A.400(2) defines “unwarranted” to mean without justification or adequate reason.
3 Examples of accouterments of public office include “uniforms, badges, official stationery, address,
photographs of public offices and other indicia of government property.” In re Public Officer, Comm’n Op.
No. 19-124A (2020).
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 10 of 20

The Commission has specifically held that the use of official government social
media to promote a public officer’s private interests, including their campaign for public
office, is an unwarranted privilege under NRS 281A.400(2). See Seaman. In Seaman, the
Commission found:
Seaman is advised that featuring social media accounts that promote her
mayoral campaign on City funded and produced programs on KCLV or on
fliers for City sponsored events would violate NRS 281A.400(2) and (7)
and NRS 281A.520.
Id., at p.6. The Commission has similarly held that a member of the board of a public
entity would violate NRS 281A.400(2) by using their public position to promote videos or
websites during a public board meeting, as they would improperly be using their official
position to further their private interest in maintaining political support. See In re Public
Officer, Comm’n Op. No. 25-003A (2025) (“25-003A”). The Commission has also held
that it is a violation of NRS 281A.400(2) for a county commissioner to use time during a
county commission meeting to promote their private interests “because such comments
may be afforded greater significance or weight when they are delivered by a public official,
especially when referencing his public position or acting in an official capacity.” In re
Gilman, Comm’n Op. No. 14-73C (2016), at pp. 7-8 (Gilman”).
Anthony directed LG Office and OSBA staff to use government staff, time and
resources to develop content for his personal @StavrosAnthony social media account,
promoting his personal political interests and his reelection campaign. Anthony further
used LT Office and OSBA staff, time and resources to repost and amplify social media
posts in support of his reelection campaign on the LG Office and OSBA official
government social media accounts.
By using government time, staff and resources, including official government social
media accounts, to bolster his reelection campaign, Anthony granted himself the
unwarranted privilege of using public money and resources to support his reelection
campaign. See 19-124A. Anthony also created the impression of official government
sanction of his reelection campaign by promoting his campaign using his public position
and access to official government accounts. See 25-003A; Seaman; Gilman.
Any candidate for office, including those running against Anthony for Lieutenant
Governor, would certainly like to have their private interests and campaign events and
activities amplified out to all official government office social media account followers and
use state staff and resources, and therefore public money, to create content for their
personal campaign social media platforms. However, the Ethics Law prohibits public
officers from granting themselves the unwarranted privilege and advantage of using
public money and official government channels, to which they only have access due to
their public position, to promote their own campaign or any political endorsement. NRS
281A.400(2).
Accordingly, the Commission determines, based on a preponderance of the
evidence, that Anthony violated NRS 281A.400(2) by using government staff, time and
resources to create and post his personal social media posts and to repost and amplify
his campaign social media posts on the LG Office and OSBA official government
accounts. The Commission therefore grants the Executive Director’s Motion for Summary
Judgment as to Anthony’s violation of NRS 281A.400(2).
Opinion
Case No. 25-024C
Page 11 of 20

B. VIOLATION OF NRS 281A.400(7) – IMPROPER USE OF GOVERNMENT
RESOURCES AND PROPERTY
As relevant here, NRS 281A.400(7) prohibits a public officer from using
governmental time, property, equipment or other facility to benefit his own significant
personal or pecuniary interest. At issue in this matter is whether Anthony’s use of state
staff time, state computer systems and email and official government social media
accounts to (1) amplify his private personal campaign social media account and interests;
and (2) establish, coordinate, launch, and defend the Task Force violated NRS
281A.400(7).
The Executive Director argues that Anthony has a significant personal interest in
both the Task Force and his reelection campaign and that he violated NRS 281A.400(7)
by using state staff, time and resources to support his personal interest. The Executive
Director also argues that Anthony’s conduct is the modern version of previous
Commission decisions finding that the use of state paid staff to prepare and mail letters
on official letterhead in support of a public officer’s personal interest is a violation of NRS
281A.400(7) because the official LG Office’s official social media account is the equivalent
to digital letterhead.
Anthony argues there is no evidence or authority to show that his use of
government time, staff or resources in support of the Task Force and his personal
campaign social media account benefited his significant pecuniary interest.4 The
Commission disagrees as the language of NRS 281A.400(7) requires that either
Anthony’s personal or pecuniary interest is benefited by the use of governmental time,
property or equipment.
1. Significant Personal Interest in Reelection Campaign and Task
Force
The Commission has repeatedly found that a candidate running for public office
has a significant personal and financial interest in being elected to the position sought,
holding that “[c]ampaigns and political support are private interests that often converge
with public duties.” 19-124A. Specifically incumbent public officers seeking re-election
have significant personal and financial interests in maintaining the elected position.
Antinoro, at p. 5. The Commission therefore finds based on a preponderance of the
evidence that Anthony has a significant personal interest in his campaign for reelection.
4
Anthony also argues that he has a First Amendment right to create, support and speak in favor of the
Task Force or any campaign. Although Anthony’s message or speech are protected by the First
Amendment and are not regulated by the Ethics Law, the mechanism by which the message was delivered,
including the use of government property and resources, is not protected by the First Amendment. See In
re Public Officer, Comm’n Op. No. 19-124A (2020). The Commission has held that “all individuals enjoy a
constitutional right to speak out on political concerns.” In re Hettrick, Comm’n Op. No. 01-10 (2001), at p.
2. However, the Ethics Law prohibits the use of governmental property, including official letterhead, to
benefit a significant personal interest, especially when such use creates the impression that the government
sanctions the activity. See id. Anthony’s First Amendment right to create, support and speak in favor of the
Task Force using his official title does not entitle him to use government resources, including official
government social media accounts, to support his private interest in the Task Force or any campaign.

As to the Task Force, Anthony asserts that he does not have a personal interest
in the Task Force but that it is an official part of his public office as the Lieutenant
Governor. Anthony argues that because there is no statute, rule, regulation, policy or
other authority that prohibits the Lieutenant Governor from advocating on political issues,
supporting political causes or legislation or from specifically forming the Task Force
proves that his involvement in the Task Force is a proper exercise of his discretionary
power. The Commission disagrees.
The relevant legal question in determining whether Anthony has a significant
personal interest in the Task Force is whether the Task Force is a governmental interest
of the LG Office or OSBA or if it is a significant personal interest of Anthony. The
Commission has interpreted “significant” to mean any non-trivial or non-de minimis
interest. See In re Carter, Comm’n Op. No. 19-016A (2019), at p. 6. The Commission has
held that:
[T]he descriptive terms of "significant" and "personal" interest are defined by
their plain meaning to be a personal interest that is important rather than
incidental, trivial or de minimus… Public officers and employees have “a
significant personal interest in endorsing a political candidate, which private
interest is of such importance as to be protected by the First Amendment of the
U.S. Constitution.” In re Antinoro, Comm'n Op. No. 16-54C (2017), at p. 4.
In re Public Officer, Comm’n Op. No. 19-124A (2020). A significant personal interest is
therefore any important non-de minimis interest that is not related to the interests of the
government office.
The facts show that neither Anthony nor the staff of the LG Office or the OSBA
considered the Task Force to be part of either office nor was it treated by Anthony or his
staff as part of Anthony’s office or official duties. Anthony never requested state funding
for the activities of the Task Force, he never sought any statutory changes to establish
the Task Force and he never presented the work of the Task Force to any of the boards
or commissions he sits on as Lieutenant Governor.
Anthony was further unable to point to any constitutional or statutory duty of the
Lieutenant Governor that would allow him to create and fund the Task Force. The duties
and responsibilities of the Lieutenant Governor have been identified by the Nevada
Legislature as follows:
The Lieutenant Governor is elected for a four-year term. The Lieutenant
Governor is the highest officer in the state after the Governor and serves as
Acting Governor when the governor is out of state or temporarily
incapacitated. The Lieutenant Governor's executive duties include serving
as Chairman of the Commission on Tourism, Vice-Chairman of the State
Board of Transportation, a member of the Board of the Governor's Office of
Economic Development, and a member of the Executive Budget Audit
Committee. Additionally, the Lieutenant Governor serves as an appointed
member to the Governor's Commission on Homeland Security and
Chairman of the Cyber Security Subcommittee. The Lieutenant Governor is
the only elected official with specific duties and powers in two branches of
state government: the executive and legislative branches. When the State
Legislature convenes for its biennial sessions, the Lieutenant Governor
serves as the President of the Senate. Although the Lieutenant Governor is
the Senate's presiding officer, he is not a member and cannot vote on any

question or legislative measure except to break a tie. Additionally, the
Lieutenant Governor can pursue up to three legislative initiatives during
regular sessions.
See Nevada Constitution, Article 5, Section 17 and 18; NRS Chapter 224.5 None of the
identified duties or responsibilities allow Anthony to create or coordinate the Task Force
through the staff and resources of the LG Office or the OSBA.
Anthony’s responses to discovery in this matter and his testimony before the Joint
Meeting of the Senate Committee on Finance and Assembly Committee on Ways and
Means shows that the Task Force was created as a result of Anthony’s personal interest
in and passion for the issues addressed by the Task Force and his personal desire to see
legislation passed regarding those issues. Anthony has not proposed or sponsored any
such legislation, and the work of the Task Force was primarily limited to lobbying the
Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association for rule changes.
Anthony also argues that because the purpose of the Task Force is to advocate
for legislation, the Task Force is not his personal interest. A “campaign” as referenced in
the Ethics Law includes not only campaigns in support of a candidate for office, but the
Commission has explicitly held that campaigns also include efforts in support of ballot
initiatives and petition campaigns6. See In re Public Officer, Comm’n Op. No. 25-206A
(2025).
The Commission therefore finds based on a preponderance of the evidence that
Anthony has a significant personal interest in the Task Force.
2. Violation of NRS 281A.400(7)
The Commission has repeatedly held that “[c]ampaigns and political support are
private interests that often converge with public duties.” In re Public Officer, Comm’n Op.
No.19-124A (2020). “Simply, public officers and employees are not entitled to take
advantage of public resources to support their own campaign or other political
campaigns.” Antinoro, at p. 4; see also Seaman, at p. 7; In re Matson, Comm’n Op. No
14-70C (2014) (“Matson”), at p. 11.
The facts show that Anthony directed LG Office and OSBA staff to use government
time, staff and resources to repost and amplify campaign posts from his personal
@StavrosAnthony social media account on the LG Office and OSBA official government
social media account in support of his personal interest in his reelection campaign for
Lieutenant Governor. The Commission therefore finds based on a preponderance of the
evidence that Anthony’s use of state-paid staff and state time and resources to create
and post social media posts to his private campaign account in support of his reelection
campaign is a violation of NRS 281A.40097).

The Commission has also previously held that use of official public office letterhead
to promote the personal political interest of a public officer is a violation of NRS
281A.400(7) because official letterhead is government property. In re Hammargren,
Comm’n Op. No. 95-35 (1996) (“Hammargren”). In Hammargren, the Commission found
that the then-lieutenant governor’s use of state-paid staff to prepare and mail a letter on
official letterhead to garner support regarding proposed legislation violated NRS
281A.400(7).
The Commission finds that Anthony’s use of official government social media
accounts to promote his significant personal interests in his reelection campaign and the
Task Force was a violation of NRS 281A.400(7). Similarly to official public office
letterhead, official government social media accounts that state that they are the official
social media account for a public office, link to the official government website for that
office and/or are maintained by government-paid staff are government property. Official
government social media accounts therefore can only be used for proper government
purposes and cannot be used to promote a public officer’s private interests.
The facts show that Anthony directed state-paid staff to use state time, resources
and computer systems to create and support the Task Force and to create and post social
media posts in support of the Task Force on official government social media accounts.
Anthony also directed state-paid staff to repost his personal campaign social media posts
in support of his reelection campaign on official government social media accounts.7 On
this basis, the Commission finds based on a preponderance of the evidence that Anthony
also violated NRS 281A.400(7).
The Commission therefore grants the Executive Director’s Motion for Summary
Judgment and finds that Anthony committed two violations of NRS 281A.400(7) for using
of state staff time, state computer systems and email and official government social media
accounts to (1) amplify Anthony’s private personal campaign social media account and
interests; and (2) establish, coordinate, launch, and defend the Task Force.8
C. NO VIOLATION OF NRS 281A.400(9) – USE OF GOVERNMENT
POSITION TO ATTEMPT TO BENEFIT PERSONAL OR PECUNIARY
INTERESTS THROUGH INFLUENCE OF A SUBORDINATE
To find a violation of NRS 281A.400(9), the facts must establish by a
preponderance of the evidence: (1) that the subject is a public officer or employee; (2)
who attempts to benefit their significant personal or pecuniary interest; (3) through the
influence of a subordinate.
The evidence presented in this matter does not support a finding based on a
preponderance of the evidence that Anthony attempted to influence any subordinate in
order to benefit his personal or pecuniary interest. The Commission therefore grants
Anthony’s Motion for Summary Judgment as to any violation of NRS 281A.400(9).

D. WILLFULNESS
Pursuant to NRS 281A.170, a violation is willful if it is intentional and knowing,
which terms are defined in NRS 281A.105 and NRS 281A.115 respectively. For an act
to be intentional, NRS 281A.105 requires that the subject acted “voluntarily and
deliberately.” “The term does not require proof of bad faith, ill will, evil intent or malice.”
NRS 281A.105. Here, Anthony directed the use of government staff, time and resources
to repost and amplify his personal campaign social media account to the LG Office and
OSBA official government social media accounts. His conduct was therefore neither
accidental nor inadvertent but rather was intentional as defined in NRS 281A.105.
“‘Knowingly imports a knowledge that the facts exist which constitute the act or
omission, and does not require knowledge of the prohibition against the act or omission.”
NRS 281A.115. The provisions of NRS Chapter 281A do not require Anthony to have
actual knowledge that his conduct violated the Ethics Law. See State v. Rhodig, 101 Nev.
608, 611, 707 P.2d 549, 551 (1985) (“[T]he law does not require knowledge that such an
act or omission is unlawful.”). Here, Anthony was aware of the facts constituting the
violations, and Commission precedent has consistently established that use of
government property, resources and time in support of a public officer’s personal interests
can lead to violations of NRS 281A.400(2) and (7).
Therefore, the Commission finds, based on a preponderance of the evidence, that
Anthony’s conduct in using government time, property and resources to repost and
amplify his personal campaign social media account, constituting one violation of NRS
281A.400(7), was knowing and therefore willful. The Commission finds that Anthony’s
remaining violations of NRS 281A.400(2) and (7) were non-willful.
E. NRS 281A.775 – MITIGATING FACTORS AND CIVIL PENALTY
The Commission considers all relevant mitigating factors set forth in NRS
281A.775 in determining whether a violation is willful and, if so, any civil penalty to be
imposed. However, each factor may not necessarily be present or be provided equal
weight.
1. Seriousness of the violation. As indicated above, the Commission has
issued several opinions establishing that public officers cannot use
government time, resources or property in support of their personal
interests.
2. The number and history of previous violations. Anthony has no prior history
of Ethics Law violations.
3. The cost to conduct the investigation and hearing. This case proceeded
through jurisdictional reviews, investigation, review panel determination,
dispositive motion practice, and a dispositive motion hearing, leading to
additional cost to the Commission.
4. Mitigating factors. Anthony did not self-report or seek any advisory opinions
from the Commission prior to creating the Task Force and using
government time, resources or property in support of the Task Force and
his personal campaign social media account.

5. Restitution and reimbursement. No restitution or reimbursement was
warranted in this matter
6. Extent of financial gain. Anthony has not yet been reelected to the position
of Lieutenant Governor.
The nature of the violations and the totality of Anthony’s conduct is determined to
be significant when measured against the public’s trust and the public policy of the State
of Nevada requiring that public officers and employees not use government property for
their benefit. Based upon the record, the Commission determines that Anthony’s conduct
constitutes one non-willful violation of NRS 281A.400(2) and one willful violation and one
non-willful violation of NRS 281A.400(7).
Pursuant to NRS 281A.790(1), the Commission may, in addition to any other
penalties, impose civil penalties as follows:
(a) Not to exceed $5,000 for a first willful violation of this
chapter;
(b) Not to exceed $10,000 for a separate act or event that
constitutes a second willful violation of this chapter; and
(c) Not to exceed $25,000 for a separate act or event that
constitutes a third willful violation of this chapter.
The Commission is authorized to take any combination of remedies and penalties that
the Commission “determines will remedy the violation or alleged violation or deter similar
violations or conduct.” NRS 281A.785(1)(c). Based on the finding of one willful violation,
the Commission imposes a civil penalty of $3,000 for Anthony’s willful violation of NRS
281A.400(7). The Commission further imposes a requirement that Anthony attend ethics
training and develop a social media policy for the LG Office and the OSBA. NRS
281A.785(1)(a)(2) and (c).
V. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. At all times relevant to this matter, Anthony was a “public officer” as defined
by NRS 281A.160.
2. Pursuant to NRS 281A.280, the Commission has jurisdiction to render an
opinion in this matter.
3. Anthony, as a public officer, has a duty under the Ethics Law and its
interpretive opinions to maintain proper separation between public duties
and private interests. See NRS 281A.020.
4. Pursuant to NRS 281A.400(2), Anthony, as a public officer, is prohibited
from using his position in government to secure an unwarranted advantage
for himself.
5. Based upon the preponderance of the evidence, Anthony committed one
non-willful violation of NRS 281A.400(2) by using government staff, time
and resources to create and post his personal social media posts and to
repost and amplify his campaign social media posts on the LG Office and
OSBA official government accounts.

Commissioners Moran and Smith, dissenting:
After reviewing the pleadings, evidence, and applicable law, we voted to deny the
Executive Director’s motion for summary judgment and we would have granted summary
judgment in favor of the Lieutenant Governor.
The statutes relied on by the Executive Director—NRS 281A.400(2), (7), and (9)—
each require proof that the public officer had a “significant personal interest” and used or
attempted to use his official position to benefit that interest. The subsections relied upon
state:
2. A public officer or employee shall not use the public officer’s or
employee’s position in government to secure or grant unwarranted
privileges, preferences, exemptions or advantages for the public
officer or employee, any business entity in which the public officer or
employee has a significant pecuniary interest or any person to whom
the public officer or employee has a commitment in a private
capacity. As used in this subsection, “unwarranted” means without
justification or adequate reason.
7. [. . .], a public officer or employee shall not use governmental
time, property, equipment or other facility to benefit a significant
personal or pecuniary interest of the public officer or employee or
any person to whom the public officer or employee has a
commitment in a private capacity. [. . .]
9Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law are set forth separately in this Opinion as required by NRS
233B.125, NRS 281A.765, and NAC 281A.473; however, they are deemed interchangeable for interpretive
purposes. See State, Dep’t of Commerce v. Soeller, 98 Nev. 579, 586, 656 P.2d 224, 228 (1982)
(concluding that when “the conclusion itself gives notice of the facts on which the Commission relied . . .
we may imply the necessary factual findings, so long as the record provides substantial evidence to support
the Commission’s conclusion”).
Opinion

9. A public officer or employee shall not attempt to benefit a
significant personal or pecuniary interest of the public officer or
employee or any person to whom the public officer or employee has
a commitment in a private capacity through the influence of a
subordinate.
We do not find these standards were met.
The evidence revealed during the discovery phase of this matter showed that the
creation of the task force originated with a staff recommendation, not with the Lieutenant
Governor advancing a personal agenda. Specifically, testimony and documentary
evidence established that a staff member made the suggestion to create a task force after
observing similar efforts in other states and believing such an initiative could benefit
Nevadans. This recommendation was corroborated by emails that pre-dated the creation
of the task force and multiple witnesses. (ED Exhibit 179; Johnson Depo. Tran. at 12;
Pamintuan Depo. Tran. at 14:14-25.)
To try to establish the legal element requiring “a significant personal interest,” the
Executive Director relied primarily on the Lieutenant Governor’s statement that he was
“passionate” about protecting female athletes, as well as references to publicly reported
events involving women’s athletics. (ED Interrogatory Response No. 7.) We do not find
that “passion” for a public policy issue, standing alone, constitutes a “significant personal
interest” under the ethics statutes. There is no evidence of any unique private benefit, or
personal advantage to the Lieutenant Governor arising from the creation of the task force.
The Lieutenant Governor did not receive any benefit that was not shared equally with
others who have the same “passion” or interest in the topic.
Further, there is no precedent establishing that general policy advocacy or
expressed personal conviction meets the statutory definition of a significant personal
interest. All elected officials have (or should have) “passion” for public policy issues.
Indeed, that is why they seek to be, and are, elected to office. The Commission Opinions
cited by the Executive Director involve direct, tangible personal benefits and are
inapposite and distinguishable from the facts presented here. See e.g., In re Antinoro,
No. 17-12C (2019) (securing preferable child custody visitation for own family member).
Accordingly, we did not find any violation of NRS 281A.400(2), (7), or (9). The
record supports that the task force was created as an initiative intended to serve a public
purpose10, not to benefit any significant personal interest of the Lieutenant Governor. For
these reasons, we dissent from our colleagues on this matter. We would have granted
summary judgment in favor of the Lieutenant Governor.
